newsitem.title: JAPAN: Profits seen forging ahead at Japan steelmakers.
newsitem.headline: Profits seen forging ahead at Japan steelmakers.

text.p: Most of Japan's major steelmakers are expected to enjoy rising profits this fiscal year after a solid performance in the just-ended period, helped by the weak yen and a possible rise in sales prices to big customers.
Analysts said the steelmakers were expected to turn in higher profits for the fiscal year which ended on March 31 and that earnings should stay on an upward trend in the current business year.

"Despite flat or slightly lower crude steel output this year, the current profits of major steelmakers in 1997/98 are expected to be bigger than 1996/97 because of rationalisation and a possible increase in the selling price to large customers in the construction, electronics, and automobile industries," said Yasuo Fujiwara, senior analyst at Kankaku Research.

Nippon Steel Corp, NKK Corp, Sumitomo Metal Industries Ltd and Kawasaki Steel Corp are expected to have posted higher parent current profits in the year ended March 31, while Kobe Steel's profit is seen down from the previous year, analysts said.
They said all of the steelmakers, with the exception of Kobe Steel, will continue to enjoy strong profit growth in 1997/98. Kobe's profit is expected to hold steady in the current business year.
The steelmakers will announce their earnings forecasts for this year as well as their earnings for the past business year on Thursday.
Analysts said they expect steelmakers' 1996/97 profits to be little changed from the estimates the firms made in March.

In March, Nippon Steel estimated a parent current profit of 83 billion yen, NKK 34 billion yen, Kobe Steel 27 billion yen, Sumitomo Metal Industries 22 billion yen and Kawasaki Steel 23 billion yen. In 1995/96, Nippon Steel's current profit was 64.70 billion yen, NKK 30.32 billion yen, Kobe Steel 36.04 billion yen, Sumitomo Metal 20.25 billion yen and Kawasaki Steel 16.63 billion yen.
Nikko Research analyst Kazuhiro Harada echoed Fujiwara's view on the earnings outlook for the steelmakers.
"Firmness in spot market prices will contribute to profits while the weak yen will offer some benefits," Harada said.
The yen's weakness against the dollar over the past year has helped steelmakers' boost exports and overall earnings due to foreign exchange gains, analysts said.
"The yen is still weak against the dollar," Harada said.
In March, the steelmakers disclosed their profit targets for 1997/98 when they revised their forecasts for 1996/97.

Nippon Steel said it was targeting a parent current profit of more than 100 billion yen in 1997/98. NKK said it expected profits to be the same or above the level reached in 1996/97. Kobe Steel said it aimed to post a parent current profit of more than 30 billion yen.
Harada expects Kobe Steel to post flat profits because of uncertainty over the profitability of its machinery division.
He expects the firms to revise their 1997/98 earnings estimates later on in the year.
"They may revise up their 1997/98 prospects by September or after because of a possible increase in the selling price for large-lot users," he said.
Harada said he does not think steelmakers have reached agreement on a rise in steel prices with large-lot customers yet, but a deal could be clinched around September.
Steelmakers lowered their selling prices for large customers over the last five years following the appreciation of the yen against the dollar.
Kankaku's Fujiwara estimated Nippon Steel's current profit at 140 billion yen in 1997/98.
Harada said Nippon Steel's current profit will range from 130 billion yen to 150 billion yen, in view of the current yen/dollar rate.
